lesson.title: Equal Partners: Nonpolar Covalent Bonds
lesson.summary: When two bonded atoms pull on their shared electrons with essentially equal strength, the result is a nonpolar covalent bond, with no meaningful partial charge building up on either atom.
lesson.body:
A nonpolar covalent bond sits at the low end of the electronegativity difference scale, conventionally below about delta EN 0.4. In this range, the two bonded atoms attract the shared electron pair with such similar strength that the electron density stays essentially centered between them, and neither atom develops a partial charge worth writing down. This is the opposite end of the same continuum that runs through polar covalent bonds toward fully ionic bonds.

The purest possible case of a nonpolar covalent bond is a bond between two atoms of the exact same element, where delta EN is precisely zero by definition, since the two atoms are, by identity, equally electronegative. The diatomic elements are the clearest examples: the H-H bond in H2, the N triple bond N in N2, the O=O bond in O2, and the Cl-Cl bond in Cl2 are all perfectly nonpolar homonuclear bonds, regardless of how electronegative or non electronegative that particular element happens to be on its own.

Carbon-hydrogen bonds are the most chemically important nonpolar covalent bonds involving two different elements. With a delta EN of about 0.35, just under the conventional cutoff, C-H bonds are treated as essentially nonpolar even though carbon and hydrogen are not literally identical atoms. This single fact underlies an enormous amount of organic chemistry: hydrocarbons such as methane and hexane, built almost entirely from C-H and C-C bonds, behave overall as nonpolar molecules, which is why they mix easily with oils and other nonpolar substances but resist mixing with water. Carbon-carbon bonds reinforce this picture directly: since both atoms are carbon, their delta EN is exactly zero, making every C-C bond perfectly nonpolar in exactly the same way as the diatomic elements. That leaves the C-H bonds as the only, and still very weak, source of bond dipoles anywhere in a simple hydrocarbon.

It is worth contrasting nonpolar covalent bonds directly against the polar covalent bonds covered just before this concept: the underlying physical cause, unequal versus equal pulling power between two nuclei, is identical in both cases, and only the size of the electronegativity gap differs. Nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, and ionic bonding are not separate mechanisms but three labeled regions along one single scale of electronegativity difference.

A molecule built entirely out of nonpolar bonds is guaranteed to be a nonpolar molecule overall, since there is no meaningful bond dipole anywhere in the structure for geometry to arrange or cancel. Diatomic O2 and N2 are trivially nonpolar this way. Methane is nonpolar for the same underlying reason, since all four of its bonds are the essentially nonpolar C-H type, and its perfectly symmetric tetrahedral shape reinforces that outcome rather than creating it from scratch. Molecules that mix polar and nonpolar bonds, or that have only polar bonds arranged asymmetrically, are a more interesting case, and that is precisely where dipole moment picks up the story.
